content.title: About
content.content: Baby Toddler Yogurt Melts are soft, melt‑in‑the‑mouth treats designed for children from 12 months old. They are made from natural yogurt enriched with calcium, vitamin D and probiotics, and contain a small amount of fruit puree for a gentle flavor.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Each melt weighs about 5 g and provides roughly 30 kcal.
The product contains no artificial colors or flavors.
The yogurt base is heat‑treated to preserve beneficial probiotics.
Melts dissolve quickly in the mouth, reducing choking risk for toddlers.
Packages usually contain 10–12 pieces, convenient for on‑the‑go snacking.

items.title: Supports bone health
items.content: Calcium and vitamin D help strengthen developing bones in young children.

items.title: Probiotic action
items.content: Added probiotics aid in maintaining a healthy gut microbiome.

items.title: Source of protein
items.content: Yogurt provides easily digestible protein needed for growth.

items.title: Low sugar content
items.content: Sweetness comes from natural fruit puree, without refined sugar.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Yogurt supplies vitamins B2 and B12, important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: The product contains milk protein and may trigger reactions in children allergic to dairy.

items.title: Lactose content
items.content: Children with lactose intolerance may experience discomfort after consumption.

items.title: Heat exposure
items.content: Storing in high temperatures can affect texture and flavor.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Give a melt to the child straight from the package. It dissolves quickly, so no chewing is required. Serve as a standalone snack or pair with fruit puree.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in a dry, cool place away from direct sunlight. Once opened, consume within 7 days.

content.title: About
content.content: Beef neck bones are bones taken from the neck section of a cow. They are rich in gelatin, collagen, and minerals, making them an excellent base for stocks, soups, and stews. The bones are usually sold whole, in sections, or with a small amount of attached meat.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Neck bones contain more gelatin than bones from other parts of the animal because of their high collagen content.
They are a classic ingredient in French bone broth (bouillon de os).
Long simmering releases glucosamine and chondroitin, compounds beneficial for joint health.
In some cuisines the bones are roasted before boiling to deepen flavor.
Beef neck bones are often used in restorative recipes after illness due to their nutrient density.

items.title: Rich in gelatin
items.content: Gelatin supports digestive health by strengthening the stomach lining and aiding nutrient absorption.

items.title: Source of collagen
items.content: Collagen helps maintain skin elasticity, hair strength, and nail health.

items.title: Mineral content
items.content: The bones provide calcium, phosphorus, and magnesium, essential for bone and nerve function.

items.title: Amino acids
items.content: Beef bones supply glycine and proline, which are important for connective‑tissue repair.

items.title: Joint support
items.content: Glucosamine and chondroitin released during cooking may aid joint comfort and mobility.

items.title: High sodium potential
items.content: If the bones are pre‑salted, the resulting broth can be high in sodium.

items.title: Beef allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to beef products.

items.title: Contamination risk
items.content: Improper storage can lead to bacterial growth; keep bones refrigerated or frozen.

items.title: Digestibility
items.content: Large bone pieces can be hard to digest; long simmering and straining are recommended.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Place the bones in cold water, bring to a gentle boil, then reduce heat and simmer for 6–12 hours. Add vegetables, herbs, and spices for flavor. After cooking, strain the broth to remove bones and solids.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Fresh bones can be kept in the refrigerator for up to 2 days. For longer storage, freeze them in airtight bags for up to 6 months. Thaw in the fridge, and keep cooked broth refrigerated for no more than 3 days.

content.title: About
content.content: Evaporated milk, NS (no fat) is a concentrated dairy product made by removing water from skimmed milk until it reaches a thick, sweet consistency. It contains no fat but retains most of the milk’s nutrients, including protein, calcium, and B‑vitamins.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Evaporated milk was invented in the 19th century to allow milk to be stored without refrigeration.
Removing the fat gives the product a longer shelf life and lower calorie content compared with regular sweetened condensed milk.
NS‑type evaporated milk is often used in diet plans and recipes that need sweetness without added fat.
In Russia and CIS countries the product is commonly labeled “NS” (no fat).
The milk can be easily reconstituted with hot water, making it convenient for drinks.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Provides about 8 g of protein per 100 g, supporting muscle maintenance.

items.title: Calcium source
items.content: Delivers a significant portion of the daily calcium requirement for bone and teeth health.

items.title: Low fat content
items.content: Absence of fat makes it suitable for low‑fat and calorie‑controlled diets.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Contains riboflavin (B2) and vitamin B12, which are important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Quick energy source
items.content: Sweet taste and simple sugars provide fast‑acting energy, useful in sports nutrition.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: The product is sweetened, which can be problematic for people with diabetes or those monitoring weight.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: Contains lactose, so it is not suitable for individuals with lactose intolerance.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: People allergic to casein or whey may experience reactions.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Despite being fat‑free, it remains calorie‑dense due to sugar.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: NS evaporated milk can be added to coffee, tea, porridge, smoothies, used in baking, desserts, and sauces. It can also be diluted with water to make a sweet milk drink.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in a cool, dry place in a tightly sealed container. After opening, keep refrigerated and consume within 2–3 weeks.

peas-and-carrots-frozen-cooked-fat-added.title: Peas and carrots, frozen, cooked, fat added

content.title: About
content.content: Peas and carrots are a frozen vegetable blend that has been heat‑treated and enriched with a small amount of vegetable oil. The mix is ready to eat after reheating and retains most of the vitamins and minerals found in fresh vegetables.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The blend is commonly used in school cafeterias and ready‑meal products.
Freezing locks in bright colour and a crisp texture.
Added fat enhances flavour and improves absorption of fat‑soluble vitamins A and K.
Peas are a good source of plant protein, while carrots provide provitamin A (beta‑carotene).
The product is usually packed in airtight bags, giving a shelf life of up to 12 months.

items.title: Rich in plant protein
items.content: Peas contain about 5 g of protein per 100 g, making the blend a solid protein source for vegetarians.

items.title: Supports eye health
items.content: Beta‑carotene from carrots is converted to vitamin A, essential for good vision.

items.title: Provides dietary fibre
items.content: The vegetables supply fibre that aids digestion and promotes satiety.

items.title: Fat‑soluble vitamins
items.content: The added oil helps the body absorb vitamins A, D, E and K more efficiently.

items.title: Low sodium content
items.content: When no extra salt is added, the product fits well into low‑sodium diets.

items.title: Pea allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to peas, ranging from skin rash to anaphylaxis.

items.title: Fat content
items.content: Although the added fat is modest, the product still contributes calories, so portion control is advised.

items.title: Anti‑nutrients
items.content: Peas contain phytic acid, which in large amounts can reduce mineral absorption.

items.title: Proper heating required
items.content: Insufficiently heated product may retain microbial hazards.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Reheat the blend in the microwave for 2–3 minutes or quickly sauté in a pan. It can be added to soups, stews, pasta dishes, or served as a side to meat and fish.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the frozen mix at –18 °C or lower. Once thawed, consume within 24 hours and do not store in the refrigerator for more than 2 days.

content.title: About
content.content: Persimmon is an orange, sweet fruit of the Diospyros kaki tree, native to China. Today it is grown in Japan, Korea, the Mediterranean, the Caucasus, and Central Asia. Ripe persimmon has tender, honey-like flesh. There are astringent varieties, which are eaten only when completely soft, and non-astringent ones, which can be eaten firm like an apple.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The genus name Diospyros can be translated from Greek as "food of the gods."
The astringent taste of unripe persimmon comes from tannins, which disappear as the fruit ripens.
Sharon fruit is a persimmon variety without seeds or an astringent taste.
In Japan, persimmons are made into dried fruits called hoshigaki.
Persimmons ripen in autumn, and the fruits often stay on the branches after the trees have dropped their leaves.

items.title: Contains carotenoids
items.content: Carotenoids give persimmons their color, and the body converts some of them into vitamin A.

items.title: Contains vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C supports the immune system and skin.

items.title: Source of fiber
items.content: Fiber supports digestion and helps you feel full.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: The tannins and flavonoids in persimmons have antioxidant properties.

items.title: Contains potassium and manganese
items.content: These minerals support muscle and nerve function and metabolism.

items.title: Unripe astringent persimmon
items.content: Eating a lot of unripe astringent persimmon, especially on an empty stomach, may lead to dense clumps in the stomach (a bezoar).

items.title: Sugar
items.content: Persimmons are sweet and contain a lot of natural sugar, so people with diabetes should watch their portion size.

items.title: Potassium
items.content: People with kidney disease who need to limit potassium should check with a doctor.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Persimmon allergy is possible, including cross-reactions with some other fruits.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Astringent varieties should be eaten only when the fruit has become completely soft, for example with a spoon. Non-astringent ones, such as Sharon fruit, can be eaten firm, cut into wedges. Persimmon can be added to salads, yogurt, smoothies, desserts, and baked goods, or dried.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Leave firm persimmons at room temperature to ripen. Store ripe fruit in the refrigerator for a few days. The flesh can be frozen whole or as a puree. Keep dried persimmons in an airtight container in a cool, dry place.

pizza-cheese-with-fruit-thin-crust.title: Thin Crust Pizza with Cheese and Fruit

content.title: About
content.content: Thin crust pizza with cheese and fruit combines melted cheese, sweet fruit pieces (such as pineapple, pear or apple) and a crisp, light dough. This style is popular in Mediterranean and Asian-inspired cuisines, where fresh ingredients and a delicate texture are prized.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Fruit‑topped pizzas first appeared in the United States in the 1960s as part of the “Hawaiian” pizza experiment.
Thin crust dough is often made with little or no yeast, resulting in a crispier base.
The sweet‑salty contrast of cheese and fruit is a favorite among many food enthusiasts.
Traditional cheese for this pizza is mozzarella, but brie or gorgonzola are also used for a stronger flavor.
Fruit is sometimes added after baking to preserve its fresh aroma and texture.

items.title: Rich in calcium
items.content: Cheese provides calcium, essential for strong bones and teeth.

items.title: Vitamins from fruit
items.content: Fruits supply vitamin C, vitamin A and antioxidants that support the immune system.

items.title: Lower fat in thin crust
items.content: Thin crust typically contains less oil than traditional dough, reducing overall calories.

items.title: Protein from cheese
items.content: Cheese adds dairy protein, contributing to satiety.

items.title: Fiber from fruit
items.content: Fruit adds dietary fiber, beneficial for digestion.

items.title: Dairy allergy
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to dairy proteins found in cheese.

items.title: Sugar content in fruit
items.content: Fruit adds natural sugars, which may be a concern for people with diabetes.

items.title: High sodium
items.content: Cheese often contains salt; those monitoring sodium intake should choose low‑salt varieties.

items.title: Gluten in the crust
items.content: Thin crust is usually made from wheat flour, making it unsuitable for gluten‑free diets.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the pizza hot, cut into slices. Add fruit a few minutes before the end of baking so it warms slightly without losing freshness. Pair with a light salad or fresh herbs for a balanced meal.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store leftovers in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2–3 days. Reheat in an oven or grill to restore the crisp crust.

rice-brown-with-carrots-dark-green-veget.title: Brown Rice with Carrots, Dark Green Vegetables and Tomato‑Based Sauce, No Added Fat

content.title: About
content.content: Brown rice is a whole‑grain product that retains the bran and germ, making it more nutritious than white rice. In this dish it is combined with carrots, dark green vegetables (such as broccoli or spinach) and a fat‑free tomato‑based sauce, providing a balanced mix of complex carbs, fiber, vitamins and minerals.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Brown rice contains more fiber, B‑vitamins and magnesium than white rice.
Dark green vegetables are rich in chlorophyll, which supports the body’s detoxification processes.
Carrots are one of the best sources of beta‑carotene, a precursor of vitamin A.
Fat‑free tomato sauce retains lycopene, a powerful antioxidant that is even more bioavailable with a little fat, but still beneficial on its own.
Combining rice with vegetables provides longer satiety compared with simple carbohydrates.

items.title: Sustained Energy
items.content: The complex carbohydrates in brown rice release glucose slowly, helping maintain stable energy levels.

items.title: High Fiber Content
items.content: Fiber from rice and vegetables supports digestion and a healthy gut microbiome.

items.title: Vitamins and Minerals
items.content: Beta‑carotene from carrots, vitamin C from tomatoes, and iron from dark green vegetables support immunity and skin health.

items.title: Low Fat
items.content: No added fat makes the dish suitable for calorie‑controlled and low‑fat diets.

items.title: Antioxidant Protection
items.content: Lycopene from tomatoes and chlorophyll from greens help combat free radicals.

items.title: Rice Allergy
items.content: A small number of people may experience an allergic reaction to rice.

items.title: Phytic Acid
items.content: Brown rice contains phytic acid, which can reduce the absorption of certain minerals when consumed in excess.

items.title: Oxalate Content
items.content: Dark green vegetables like spinach can contain oxalates, which may contribute to kidney stone formation if eaten in large amounts.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the dish hot as a main course or as a side to meat, fish, or tofu. It reheats well in the microwave or on the stovetop; add a splash of water to restore moisture if needed.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the prepared dish in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. When frozen, it can be stored for up to 2 months, preferably portioned out beforehand.

roll-wheat-or-cracked-wheat-hot-dog-bun.title: Hot Dog Bun (wheat or cracked wheat)

content.title: About
content.content: A hot dog bun is a soft, slightly sweet roll made from wheat or whole‑grain flour, often with added cracked wheat for texture. It is designed to hold sausages, frankfurters and various toppings, and can also serve as a base for small sandwiches.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Traditional hot dog buns are made from white wheat flour, but whole‑grain and cracked‑wheat versions have become popular for added nutrition.
In the United States more than 50 million hot dog buns are consumed each day.
Buns are frequently brushed with a light egg wash and sprinkled with sesame or poppy seeds for flavor and appearance.
In Japan similar rolls are called “hot‑dog” and are often served with mayo and soy sauce.
The dough is proofed in a warm environment to create a light, airy crumb.

items.title: Source of carbohydrates
items.content: Buns provide a quick source of energy through easily digestible carbs.

items.title: Contains fiber (whole‑grain version)
items.content: Whole‑grain buns are rich in dietary fiber, supporting healthy digestion.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Wheat flour supplies thiamine, niacin and folate, important for metabolism.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Buns contain iron, magnesium and phosphorus, which contribute to bone and blood health.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Unlike many baked goods, hot dog buns typically contain only a small amount of fat.

items.title: Wheat allergy or gluten intolerance
items.content: People with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity may experience adverse reactions to wheat buns.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: Buns can cause a rapid rise in blood sugar, which may be problematic for diabetics.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Some recipes add salt, so those monitoring sodium intake should check the label.

items.title: Preservatives and additives
items.content: Commercial buns may contain flavor enhancers and preservatives that are not suitable for everyone.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Slice the bun lengthwise, place a hot dog inside, and add mustard, ketchup, pickles, onions, cheese or any favorite toppings. Buns also work well for small sandwiches with ham, cheese and vegetables.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep buns in an airtight bag at room temperature for up to 3 days. For longer storage, freeze them in a bag – they stay fresh for up to 2 months. Warm in the oven or toaster before serving.
